source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: LATS turns MCTS into a loop for one language model. The model is the action sampler, the value estimator and the reflection writer. There is no trained world model. The tree backs up from real environment returns, and each failed leaf gets a written reflection that is stored in memory.
numbers: Six steps: selection (UCT, exploration weight w=1), expansion (n=5 sampled actions), evaluation, simulation to a terminal state, backpropagation, reflection. Defaults n=5; k=50 trajectories (HotPotQA), k=30 (WebShop, Game of 24), 8 iterations for code.
limits: Needs an environment that allows reverting to an earlier state. The authors say so. Cost is higher than ReAct or Reflexion.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our S6 state with real feedback. The program could own the tree while the model only fills slots.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: The node value mixes an LM score with a self-consistency score: V(s) = lambda*LM(s) + (1-lambda)*SC(s). SC counts how often the same action is sampled again at the same state.
numbers: lambda=0.5 for HotPotQA and Game of 24; lambda=0.8 for programming and WebShop. Game of 24 ablation (Table 13): lambda=1, which removes self-consistency, scored lower than 0.5.
limits: Both parts are model-made and share the model's blind spots. No calibration check of the value score is given.
agent_relevance: Our G4 says sample agreement is only a hint. The LATS value is that kind of signal, so real output must outweigh it.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: HotPotQA with GPT-3.5, reasoning only (no tools). Search over sampled thoughts beats plain prompting. LATS(CoT) is the best.
numbers: Exact match: base LM 0.32, CoT 0.34, CoT-SC 0.38, ToT 0.55, RAP 0.60, LATS(CoT) 0.62. 100 questions, n=5, k=50.
limits: Only 100 questions. One run reported, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Search over thoughts gives large gains even without tools. With 100 items, gaps of a few points are noise.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: HotPotQA with GPT-3.5 and Wikipedia search (acting). LATS gets the best exact match. Starting with CoT and switching to ReAct on failure is best of all.
numbers: ReAct 0.32, ReAct best-of-k 0.38, Reflexion 0.51, ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP(ReAct) 0.54, LATS(ReAct) 0.63, LATS n=3 0.58, LATS n=10 0.65, LATS(CoT+ReAct) 0.71. 100 questions, k=50.
limits: Oracle setup (see next line). ToT and RAP get worse with ReAct than in the reasoning-only table, so naive search over actions is not enough.
agent_relevance: Cheap internal reasoning first and tools only on failure matches G1 (act on a signal).

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: The authors state they use an oracle setup for HotPotQA. The environment tells the agent whether its answer was correct when it submits one. This follows Reflexion.
numbers: Applies to the HotPotQA numbers in Tables 2, 3 and 8: 100 questions, 3 few-shot examples per method.
quote: we use an oracle setup for HotPotQA, in which the environment provides feedback about the answer's correctness
limits: This is the main internal-validity limit of the headline HotPotQA gains.
agent_relevance: Treat the HotPotQA gains as an upper bound for tasks with a free correctness oracle.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: Programming with test feedback. LATS skips simulation because each action is a whole program. The reward is the share of passed model-written tests. The best-valued program is then scored on the real test suite.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1, GPT-3.5: CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. GPT-4: base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7. MBPP GPT-3.5: CoT 54.9, ReAct 67.0, Reflexion 70.0, ToT 65.8, RAP 71.4, LATS 81.1. n=5 programs, 8 iterations, 4 generated tests.
limits: Generated tests can pass a wrong program. LATS gain over Reflexion on HumanEval shrinks from 15.7 points (GPT-3.5) to 1.7 points (GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Supports G3 (pass on something the answer was not fitted to). A shrinking gain with a stronger model says search helps most when the base model is weak.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: WebShop (50 instructions, GPT-3.5). LATS raises score and success rate over ReAct and Reflexion and beats RL-trained agents on score. Reflections were often generic and the agent got stuck in local minima.
numbers: Score/SR: ReAct 53.8/28.0, ReAct best-of-k 59.1/32.0, Reflexion 64.2/35.0, LATS 75.9/38.0. IL 59.9/29.1, IL+RL 62.4/28.7, fine-tuning 67.5/45.0, human expert 82.1/59.6. n=5, k=30.
limits: LATS success rate 38.0 is below the fine-tuned agent (45.0) and far below the expert (59.6). Only 50 instructions. Score gains are larger than success-rate gains.
agent_relevance: Gains in partial score are not gains in full task success. Claims of beating RL hold for score only.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: Game of 24 with GPT-3.5, CoT base. LATS beats ToT and RAP. The authors credit the self-consistency term in the value function.
numbers: Success rate: CoT 0.08, Reflexion 0.12, ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40, LATS(CoT) 0.44. n=5, k=30.
limits: These ToT numbers use GPT-3.5. The ToT paper itself reports 74% with GPT-4, so cross-paper numbers cannot be lined up.
agent_relevance: Compare methods only inside one table with one model.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: Ablation on HotPotQA (ReAct base). Every part matters. Removing the LM value function hurts most. Replacing MCTS by DFS hurts a lot. Removing reflection costs 5 points.
numbers: LATS full 0.63. No LM heuristic 0.37. DFS 0.42. No reflection 0.58. ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP(ReAct) 0.54. Reflexion's gain over ReAct is 0.19, but reflection adds only 0.05 inside LATS.
limits: One task, 100 questions. The w and depth ablation (Table 11) was garbled in text extraction and is not recorded.
agent_relevance: Once search is present, reflection text adds little. The value signal and the back-up of results matter more.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: Cost. LATS has the same sample complexity as ToT and RAP, O(kn), and reaches success with fewer expanded nodes. The authors admit it costs more than ReAct or Reflexion.
numbers: At matched trajectory budgets: ReAct best of 250 0.42, CoT-SC k=250 0.40, LATS n=1 k=50 0.48, ToT n=5 0.49, RAP n=5 0.54, LATS n=5 0.63. Tokens upon success: RAP about 210k, LATS about 176k and 173k. LATS used 3.55 fewer nodes than RAP and 12.12 fewer than ToT.
limits: Token counts cover successful searches only. No dollars or wall-clock time. Budgets are matched in trajectories, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Real cost for our agent must be measured in tokens and calls.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: Stated limits. LATS needs to revert to earlier states. It costs more than simple prompting. The authors recommend it for hard tasks such as programming, or when performance matters more than efficiency.
numbers: Appendix B: environment queries add minor cost, and search is said to be cheaper than using an LM as a world model (RAP).
limits: Not tested on tasks with irreversible actions or real side effects.
agent_relevance: Our S6 works only where a step can be undone or simulated. Irreversible actions need another guard.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2024; TMLR 2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first tree search run in the live web environment, not a simulator. A GPT-4o value function with self-consistency scores states. It adds a relative gain on top of a strong agent.
numbers: VisualWebArena: GPT-4o+SoM 18.9% to 26.4% (+39.7% relative). WebArena: GPT-4o 15.0% to 19.2% (+28.0%). Llama-3-70B: VWA 7.6% to 16.7% (+119.7%), WA 7.6% to 10.1% (+32.3%).
limits: Absolute levels stay low (humans: 89% VWA, 78% WA). Backtracking in a live web is not always possible.
agent_relevance: An independent test of search with a model value and real feedback. Gains are real but modest in absolute terms.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2024; TMLR 2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: More search budget helps. A re-ranking of n independent trajectories with the same value function plateaus and is worse than tree search at matched compute.
numbers: Ablation subset: no search 24.5%; budget c=5 32.0% (+30.6% relative); c=20 37.0% (+51.0%). Re-ranking plateaus near 7 runs at about 30%. Search c=5 and re-rank n=5 use about equal compute.
limits: Ablation uses a subset of VWA tasks, not the full benchmark.
agent_relevance: Search beat best-of-n at equal compute here, because it can backtrack and prune.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2024; TMLR 2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: The value function is the bottleneck. Self-consistency is essential. A ground-truth reward leaves a large gap.
numbers: Value function, ablation subset: GPT-4o without self-consistency 28.5%; with SC n=5 32.5%; n=20 37.0%; LLaVA-34B with SC n=20 30.0%; ground-truth reward 43.5%.
limits: Ground truth reward is the sparse 0/1 benchmark reward, used as an upper bound.
agent_relevance: A better value signal is worth about 6.5 points here. A real check beats any model-made score (G2, G5).

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2024; TMLR 2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Search helps most on medium tasks. Hard tasks stay hard.
numbers: VWA GPT-4o by action difficulty: easy 34.2% to 42.3% (+24%), medium 12.7% to 22.2% (+75%), hard 10.2% to 14.9% (+47%).
limits: Difficulty labels are human estimates of action count.
agent_relevance: Save search for tasks the base agent cannot do in one pass (G1).

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion is the reflection half that LATS reuses. After a failed trial the agent writes a lesson and keeps it in memory for the next trial. No weights change.
numbers: ALFWorld (134 tasks): ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 over 12 trials, while ReAct alone stalled between trials 6 and 7. HumanEval pass@1 91% with GPT-4 vs 80% baseline. Gains over baselines: +22% ALFWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval.
limits: Needs a binary success or failure signal (a heuristic in ALFWorld, tests in code).
agent_relevance: The LATS reflection step is a copy of this idea. See Huang et al. for what happens without an outside signal.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion works only if the success signal is good. Model-written tests can pass wrong code. On MBPP Python, Reflexion was worse than the baseline because of false positives.
numbers: False-positive rate of tests: 16.3% on MBPP Python vs 1.4% on HumanEval Python. Baseline pass@1 82% (HumanEval) and 80% (MBPP). HumanEval Rust, 50 hardest, GPT-4: base 0.60; no test generation 0.52; no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68.
limits: Rust ablation has only 50 problems.
agent_relevance: A pass on model-written tests is weak proof (G3). Reflection without a real test made results worse (0.52 vs 0.60).

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: The reflection gains in earlier papers, including the Reflexion setup that LATS builds on, depend on oracle labels about answer correctness. With the oracle, accuracy rises. Without it, accuracy does not.
numbers: With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
quote: the improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2-70B on three benchmarks, at most two rounds of correction. Prompts taken from the source papers.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to the LATS HotPotQA numbers. It matches G2: revise only from real output.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy. The model often flips a correct answer to a wrong one.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2). GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 and 74.7. HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 and 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 and 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Self-correction prompts may not be the best possible.
agent_relevance: The self-scoring part of LATS value has no outside ground. Keep real output in the loop.

source: Hao, Gu, Ma, Hong, Wang, Wang, Hu (2023, EMNLP) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: RAP is the MCTS predecessor that LATS compares with. The LM is both policy and simulated world model. LATS replaces the world model with real environment steps.
numbers: Blocksworld, LLaMA-33B, success at 2/4/6 steps: RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42; average success 64%. GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40. The paper reports a 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT.
limits: Small benchmark. The world model is itself an LM, so simulation errors can build up over deeper plans.
agent_relevance: Shows the value of simulated rollouts when no real environment exists. S6 with real feedback avoids world-model drift.

source: Feng, Wan, Wen, McAleer, Wen, Zhang, Wang (2023/2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: A learned value function beats a prompted LM value, even when the learned model is much smaller. This tests the weakest part of LATS, the prompted value.
numbers: BFS Path@1 accuracy. GSM8K: GPT-3.5 policy with prompted GPT-3.5 value 72.7 vs learned LLaMA2-7B value 74.0; LLaMA-SFT policy with prompted LLaMA 37.4, prompted GPT-3.5 45.8, learned 52.5. Game24: GPT-3.5 policy 15.5 vs 19.1; LLaMA-SFT policy 9.2, 21.0, 64.8.
limits: Needs training data and value training, which our no-training rule excludes. Task labels in Table 2 were read from raw text.
agent_relevance: Supports G5. A prompted self-score is weak. Without training we need checks run by code.

source: Feng, Wan, Wen, McAleer, Wen, Zhang, Wang (2023/2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: At equal token budget, self-consistency with an outcome reward model nearly matches tree search on shallow tasks. Tree search wins on deep ones.
numbers: Tree search clearly beat baselines on RLHF (depth 64) and chess endgame. On GSM8K at equal tokens only BFS greedy value search beat CoT-SC with the ORM. Among search types, MCTS was almost best on quality and compute, which shows the back-up step helps.
quote: We are surprised to see that such simple algorithms can also have outstanding performance when compared fairly.
limits: Path@1 figures hide compute differences, so the authors add equal-token comparisons.
agent_relevance: For short problems, voting plus a real check may be enough. Search pays on long horizons.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models
finding: MCTS is expensive per answer. It often needs dozens of times more generated tokens than best-of-n or weighted voting, and under weighted voting it did not do well. A cheaper tree search (REBASE) matched or beat it.
numbers: Llemma-7B with REBASE beat Llemma-34B under all tested strategies on MATH500. Small models with advanced search were Pareto-optimal on cost and accuracy.
limits: Math benchmarks with a reward model, not interactive tasks. MCTS settings may be sub-optimal.
agent_relevance: MCTS-style cost is the main risk. Compare with best-of-n at equal tokens before using search.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: With GPT-4, self-critique collapses on most tasks while a sound external verifier helps. Most of the benefit comes from the verifier being sound, not from the critique text.
numbers: Game of 24: standard prompt 5%, LLM critiquing LLM 3%, LLM with sound verifier 36% (binary feedback) or 38% (first-error feedback), plain resampling k=25 42%. Graph coloring: 16% to 2% (self) vs 38% (sound). Blocksworld: 40% to 55% (self) vs 87% (sound).
limits: GPT-4 only, three domains. Self-critique raised Blocksworld from 40% to 55%, so the collapse is not universal. Column labels were partly lost in extraction.
agent_relevance: Strongest support for G2. A sound check plus plain resampling gets most of the gain, so critique text may add little.

source: Yao, Yu, Zhao, Shafran, Griffiths, Cao, Narasimhan (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: ToT is the search-over-thoughts base of LATS (BFS or DFS with a prompted value). The parallel Tree of Thoughts subfield covers it. Only the cost point is noted here.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: CoT 4%, ToT (b=5) 74%. ToT uses about 5.5k completion tokens per case, close to 100 CoT trials (6.7k). CoT best of 100 reached 49%, IO best of 100 33%.
limits: LATS reports ToT at 0.20 with GPT-3.5, so ToT is weak when the model value prompt is weak.
agent_relevance: Search beat resampling at a similar token cost only when the model could judge states.

source: Putta, Mills, Garg, Motwani, Finn, Garg, Rafailov (2024) Agent Q: Advanced Reasoning and Learning for Autonomous AI Agents
finding: MCTS with a self-critique value plus DPO training on the search trees. Test-time search alone adds a lot on WebShop. A real booking task shows large gains.
numbers: WebShop success: xLAM base 28.6%, RFT 31.3%, DPO 37.5%, base + MCTS 48.4%, Agent Q + MCTS 50.5%, average human 50.0%. Real OpenTable booking, Llama-3-70B: zero-shot 18.6%, after training 81.7%, with online search 95.4%.
limits: Uses fine-tuning, so it is not a pure scaffold result. Dense supervision added only a modest gain on WebShop.
agent_relevance: Search alone gave +19.8 points on WebShop for a trained agent. Our agent has no training, so expect less.

source: Antoniades et al. (2024; ICLR 2025) SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement
finding: MCTS with a hybrid value function (a number plus a written critique) lifts a software agent on SWE-bench Lite for five models. A discriminator debate picks the final patch.
numbers: Resolve rate, adapted baseline to SWE-Search: GPT-4o 25.7 to 31.0 (+17%), GPT-4o-mini 13.0 to 17.0, Qwen-2.5-72B 18.0 to 24.7, Deepseek-V2.5 16.3 to 21.0, Llama-3.1-70B 13.6 to 17.7. Mean +23%. The value function chose the right solution 73% of the time; the discriminator 84%.
limits: SWE-bench Lite subset, search limited to 100 iterations. More flexible state transitions alone added only 1.4%.
agent_relevance: The same pattern on a hard real-feedback task. Selection accuracy of 73% and 84% shows the value function is imperfect even here.
